source.text: וַיְהִ֣י הַיּ֗וֹם וַיֹּ֨אמֶר יוֹנָתָ֤ן בֶּן־שָׁאוּל֙ אֶל־הַנַּ֨עַר֙ נֹשֵׂ֣א כֵלָ֔יו לְכָ֗ה וְנַעְבְּרָה֙ אֶל־מַצַּ֣ב פְּלִשְׁתִּ֔ים אֲשֶׁ֖ר מֵעֵ֣בֶר הַלָּ֑ז וּלְאָבִ֖יו לֹ֥א הִגִּֽיד׃

records.literal_gloss: And it was the day, and said Jonathan son of Saul to the young man bearing his armor, Come, and let us cross over to [the] garrison of [the] Philistines which [is] on [the] other side yonder; and to his father not he told.

en.L: And it happened one day that Jonathan son of Saul said to the young man who carried his armor, "Come, and let us cross over to the garrison of the Philistines that [is] on the other side over there." But he did not tell his father.
en.B: One day Jonathan son of Saul said to the young man who carried his armor, "Come on, let us go across to the Philistine outpost on the far side, over there." But he did not tell his father.
en.R: One day Saul's son Jonathan spoke to the young man who carried his armor and weapons. "Come on," he said. "Let us go across to the Philistine outpost over on the other side." But Jonathan did not tell his father what he was doing.

decisions.choice: it was the day: one day, on a particular day
decisions.reason: The phrase marks the start of a new scene without naming the date. It follows on from the Philistine garrison moving out to the pass of Michmash (13:23).

decisions.choice: the young man who carried his armor: a personal attendant who bore his master's weapons and fought beside him
decisions.reason: An armor-bearer carried a warrior's shield and spare weapons and stayed at his side in battle (Judges 9:54; 1 Samuel 16:21; 31:4-6). The word for "armor" covers weapons and gear of every kind.

decisions.choice: he did not tell his father: Jonathan acts without Saul's knowledge
decisions.reason: The remark prepares for what follows: Saul does not know where Jonathan is until the roll is called (verse 17), and Jonathan does not hear the oath Saul lays on the army (verse 27).

decisions.choice: outpost (Balanced, Readable)
decisions.reason: The word names a stationed post of soldiers. Literal keeps "garrison"; Balanced and Readable say "outpost", which shows that it was a forward position facing Israel.

decisions.choice: what he was doing
decisions.reason: Readable supplies the object of "tell", which the Hebrew leaves to the context.

source.text: וְשָׁא֗וּל יוֹשֵׁב֙ בִּקְצֵ֣ה הַגִּבְעָ֔ה תַּ֥חַת הָרִמּ֖וֹן אֲשֶׁ֣ר בְּמִגְר֑וֹן וְהָעָם֙ אֲשֶׁ֣ר עִמּ֔וֹ כְּשֵׁ֥שׁ מֵא֖וֹת אִֽישׁ׃

records.literal_gloss: And Saul [was] staying at [the] edge of the Gibeah under the pomegranate which [is] in Migron, and the people who [were] with him [were] about six hundred man.

en.L: And Saul [was] staying at the edge of Gibeah under the pomegranate tree that [is] in Migron, and the people who [were] with him [were] about six hundred men.
en.B: Saul was staying on the outskirts of Gibeah under the pomegranate tree at Migron, and the troops with him numbered about six hundred men.
en.R: Saul was camped at the edge of Gibeah, under the pomegranate tree at Migron. He had about six hundred men with him.

decisions.choice: Gibeah and Migron: places in Benjamin, a few miles north of Jerusalem
decisions.reason: Gibeah was Saul's home town (10:26; 11:4). The Hebrew says "the Gibeah", "the hill". Migron lay near Michmash on the road from the north (Isaiah 10:28). Saul stays back while the Philistines hold the pass.

decisions.choice: the pomegranate tree: a known landmark
decisions.reason: The article points to a tree the first readers knew. The same word is also the name Rimmon, and the rock of Rimmon was a refuge in Benjamin (Judges 20:45-47), so some take it as a place name. The plain sense, a tree, fits the picture of Saul seated under it, as Deborah sat under her palm (Judges 4:5).

decisions.choice: the people: the fighting men
decisions.reason: Here "the people" means the troops. Their number has shrunk to about six hundred since the army scattered at Gilgal (13:2, 15).

decisions.choice: troops (Balanced); men (Readable)
decisions.reason: Where "the people" are soldiers, Balanced and Readable say so. Literal keeps "the people".

source.text: וַאֲחִיָּ֣ה בֶן־אֲחִט֡וּב אֲחִ֡י אִיכָב֣וֹד׀בֶּן־פִּינְחָ֨ס בֶּן־עֵלִ֜י כֹּהֵ֧ן׀יְהוָ֛ה בְּשִׁל֖וֹ נֹשֵׂ֣א אֵפ֑וֹד וְהָעָם֙ לֹ֣א יָדַ֔ע כִּ֥י הָלַ֖ךְ יוֹנָתָֽן׃

records.literal_gloss: And Ahijah son of Ahitub, brother of Ichabod son of Phinehas son of Eli, priest of Yahweh in Shiloh, [was] bearing an ephod. And the people not knew that had gone Jonathan.

en.L: And Ahijah son of Ahitub, brother of Ichabod son of Phinehas son of Eli, the priest of {{divine_name:the LORD|Yahweh}} in Shiloh, [was] wearing an ephod. And the people did not know that Jonathan had gone.
en.B: Ahijah son of Ahitub was there, wearing an ephod. Ahitub was the brother of Ichabod son of Phinehas son of Eli, the priest of {{divine_name:the LORD|Yahweh}} at Shiloh. The troops did not know that Jonathan had gone.
en.R: Ahijah the priest was also there. He was wearing the ephod, the priest's vest used to ask God for answers. Ahijah's father was Ahitub, Ichabod's brother. Their father was Phinehas, the son of Eli, who had been {{divine_name:the LORD|Yahweh}}'s priest at Shiloh. None of the men knew that Jonathan had left.

decisions.choice: an ephod: the priestly garment used to seek an answer from God
decisions.reason: The high priest's ephod held the breastpiece with the Urim and Thummim, by which Yahweh's will was asked (Exodus 28:6-30; Numbers 27:21). Later David asks Yahweh's answer through the ephod that Abiathar brings (23:9-12; 30:7-8). The verb "bearing" can mean carrying or wearing it.

decisions.choice: the line of Eli: Ahijah is Eli's great-grandson
decisions.reason: The family tree recalls Eli's house, which Yahweh had judged (2:27-36), and Ichabod, born on the day the ark was taken (4:19-22). A priest of that house now serves beside Saul.

decisions.choice: the priest of Yahweh in Shiloh: Eli
decisions.reason: The title belongs to the last name in the list, Eli, who served at the sanctuary in Shiloh (1:3, 9).

decisions.choice: the family line in a sentence of its own
decisions.reason: The Hebrew piles up the names before the verb. Balanced and Readable state first what Ahijah was doing and then give the family line separately.

decisions.choice: the ephod, the priest's vest used to ask God for answers
decisions.reason: Readable explains the word once, and calls Ahijah "the priest" as verse 19 does.

source.text: וּבֵ֣ין הַֽמַּעְבְּר֗וֹת אֲשֶׁ֨ר בִּקֵּ֤שׁ יֽוֹנָתָן֙ לַֽעֲבֹר֙ עַל־מַצַּ֣ב פְּלִשְׁתִּ֔ים שֵׁן־הַסֶּ֤לַע מֵהָעֵ֨בֶר֙ מִזֶּ֔ה וְשֵׁן־הַסֶּ֥לַע מֵהָעֵ֖בֶר מִזֶּ֑ה וְשֵׁ֤ם הָֽאֶחָד֙ בּוֹצֵ֔ץ וְשֵׁ֥ם הָאֶחָ֖ד סֶֽנֶּה׃

records.literal_gloss: And between the passes which sought Jonathan to cross over to [the] garrison of [the] Philistines [was a] tooth of the rock from the side on this [side], and [a] tooth of the rock from the side on this [side]; and [the] name of the one [was] Bozez, and [the] name of the one [was] Seneh.

en.L: And between the passes by which Jonathan sought to cross over to the garrison of the Philistines [there was] a tooth of rock on the one side and a tooth of rock on the other side; and the name of the one [was] Bozez, and the name of the other [was] Seneh.
en.B: In the pass that Jonathan meant to cross to reach the Philistine outpost there was a rocky crag on one side and a rocky crag on the other. One was named Bozez and the other Seneh.
en.R: To reach the Philistine outpost, Jonathan had to go through a pass between two steep cliffs, one on each side. One cliff was called Bozez, and the other was called Seneh.

decisions.choice: a tooth of rock: a sharp, jutting crag
decisions.reason: Hebrew speaks of a pointed rock as a "tooth" (Job 39:28). The picture is of two rock spurs standing over the ravine.

decisions.choice: the passes: the crossing of the deep ravine between Geba and Michmash
decisions.reason: This is the pass of Michmash where the Philistine garrison had taken up its position (13:23). The plural may mean the paths down into and up out of the valley.

decisions.choice: Bozez and Seneh: names of the two crags
decisions.reason: The meaning of the names is not certain. Bozez may mean "shining" or "slippery", and Seneh is the word for a thorn bush (Exodus 3:2). They are kept as names.

decisions.choice: steep cliffs
decisions.reason: Readable says plainly what the "tooth of rock" picture describes.

source.text: הַשֵּׁ֧ן הָאֶחָ֛ד מָצ֥וּק מִצָּפ֖וֹן מ֣וּל מִכְמָ֑שׂ וְהָאֶחָ֥ד מִנֶּ֖גֶב מ֥וּל גָּֽבַע׃ס

records.literal_gloss: The tooth the one [was] a pillar from [the] north in front of Michmash, and the one from [the] south in front of Geba.

en.L: The one tooth [was] a pillar on the north in front of Michmash, and the other on the south in front of Geba.
en.B: One crag rose like a pillar on the north side, facing Michmash, and the other stood on the south side, facing Geba.
en.R: One cliff rose up on the north side, facing Michmash. The other was on the south side, facing Geba.

decisions.choice: pillar: a column of rock
decisions.reason: The word is used of the pillars on which the earth stands (2:8). Here it pictures a crag rising straight up out of the ravine.

decisions.choice: Michmash and Geba: the two camps facing each other across the ravine
decisions.reason: The Philistines were camped at Michmash on the north side, and Saul's forces at Geba on the south side (13:16). Jonathan must climb down from one side and up the other.

decisions.choice: rose like a pillar
decisions.reason: Balanced turns the noun "pillar" into a picture of the crag rising up, and supplies "stood" for the second crag.

source.text: וַיֹּ֨אמֶר יְהוֹנָתָ֜ן אֶל־הַנַּ֣עַר׀נֹשֵׂ֣א כֵלָ֗יו לְכָה֙ וְנַעְבְּרָ֗ה אֶל־מַצַּב֙ הָעֲרֵלִ֣ים הָאֵ֔לֶּה אוּלַ֛י יַעֲשֶׂ֥ה יְהוָ֖ה לָ֑נוּ כִּ֣י אֵ֤ין לַֽיהוָה֙ מַעְצ֔וֹר לְהוֹשִׁ֥יעַ בְּרַ֖ב א֥וֹ בִמְעָֽט׃

records.literal_gloss: And said Jonathan to the young man bearing his armor, Come, and let us cross over to [the] garrison of the uncircumcised the these; perhaps will act Yahweh for us, for there is not to Yahweh restraint to save by many or by few.

en.L: And Jonathan said to the young man who carried his armor, "Come, and let us cross over to the garrison of these uncircumcised; perhaps {{divine_name:the LORD|Yahweh}} will act for us, for there is no restraint for {{divine_name:the LORD|Yahweh}} to save by many or by few."
en.B: Jonathan said to the young man who carried his armor, "Come, let us cross to the post held by these uncircumcised men. It may be that {{divine_name:the LORD|Yahweh}} will act for us. Nothing can keep {{divine_name:the LORD|Yahweh}} from saving, whether by many or by few."
en.R: Jonathan said to the young man who carried his armor, "Come on, let us go over to the outpost of these Philistines, who are outside God's covenant. Maybe {{divine_name:the LORD|Yahweh}} will work for us. Nothing can stop {{divine_name:the LORD|Yahweh}} from saving, whether {{deity_pronoun:he|He}} uses many people or only a few."

decisions.choice: uncircumcised: outsiders to Yahweh's covenant
decisions.reason: Circumcision was the sign of the covenant with Abraham (Genesis 17:10-14). Calling the Philistines "uncircumcised" sets them apart as people who do not belong to Yahweh, and it carries scorn (Judges 14:3; 1 Samuel 17:26).

decisions.choice: perhaps Yahweh will act for us: trust that does not presume
decisions.reason: Jonathan does not claim to know what Yahweh will do. He is sure of Yahweh's power but leaves the outcome to him, and so asks for a sign (verses 8-10).

decisions.choice: by many or by few: Yahweh's power does not depend on numbers
decisions.reason: Yahweh had saved by Gideon's three hundred so that Israel could not boast (Judges 7:2-7). Jonathan sets two men against a garrison while Saul waits with six hundred (verse 2).

decisions.choice: Jonathan: the longer spelling of the same name
decisions.reason: Here and in verse 8 the name is spelled in its longer form, "Yehonathan", "Yahweh has given"; elsewhere it is "Yonathan". Both are the same man.

decisions.choice: Philistines, who are outside God's covenant; whether he uses many people
decisions.reason: Readable names the Philistines and explains "uncircumcised" by what it meant (m1), with the wording used again at 17:26, 36 and 31:4. It also makes Yahweh the subject of "uses", which the Hebrew implies.

source.text: וַיֹּ֤אמֶר לוֹ֙ נֹשֵׂ֣א כֵלָ֔יו עֲשֵׂ֖ה כָּל־אֲשֶׁ֣ר בִּלְבָבֶ֑ךָ נְטֵ֣ה לָ֔ךְ הִנְנִ֥י עִמְּךָ֖ כִּלְבָבֶֽךָ׃ס

records.literal_gloss: And said to him bearer of his armor, Do all that [is] in your heart; turn for yourself; here I [am] with you according to your heart.

en.L: And his armor-bearer said to him, "Do all that [is] in your heart. Turn yourself [to it]; look, I [am] with you, as your heart [is]."
en.B: His armor-bearer answered him, "Do everything you have in mind. Go ahead. I am with you, whatever you decide."
en.R: The young man answered, "Do whatever you think is best. Go ahead! I am with you all the way."

decisions.choice: all that is in your heart: everything you intend
decisions.reason: In Hebrew the heart is the seat of thought and purpose as well as feeling (2:35; 9:19). The armor-bearer gives Jonathan a free hand.

decisions.choice: turn for yourself: go ahead, take the way you choose
decisions.reason: The verb means to turn or to stretch out. With "for yourself" it tells Jonathan to set out in whatever direction he wishes. The Greek translation reads differently here ("do all that your heart inclines to"), but the sense is the same.

decisions.choice: according to your heart: of one mind with you
decisions.reason: The armor-bearer will want what Jonathan wants. The phrase is used of a person who shares another's purpose (13:14).

decisions.choice: his armor-bearer
decisions.reason: From here on the Hebrew says "the bearer of his armor", and English uses the single word "armor-bearer" for it. Readable says "the young man", as in verse 1.

source.text: וַיֹּ֨אמֶר֙ יְה֣וֹנָתָ֔ן הִנֵּ֛ה אֲנַ֥חְנוּ עֹבְרִ֖ים אֶל־הָאֲנָשִׁ֑ים וְנִגְלִ֖ינוּ אֲלֵיהֶֽם׃

records.literal_gloss: And said Jonathan, Look, we [are] crossing over to the men, and we will reveal ourselves to them.

en.L: And Jonathan said, "Look, we [are] crossing over to the men, and we will show ourselves to them.
en.B: Jonathan said, "All right, we will cross over to the men and let them see us.
en.R: Jonathan said, "Here is what we will do. We will go across toward those men and let them see us.

decisions.choice: we are crossing over: what they are about to do
decisions.reason: The participle with "look" describes an action about to happen. Jonathan sets out the plan before they move.

decisions.choice: we will reveal ourselves: come out into the open
decisions.reason: The verb means to uncover or reveal. Instead of creeping up unseen, the two will deliberately show themselves, so that the Philistines' answer can serve as a sign (verses 9-10).

decisions.choice: All right (Balanced); Here is what we will do (Readable)
decisions.reason: The word "look" here introduces a plan, so Balanced and Readable render it by what it does.

source.text: אִם־כֹּ֤ה יֹֽאמְרוּ֙ אֵלֵ֔ינוּ דֹּ֕מּוּ עַד־הַגִּיעֵ֖נוּ אֲלֵיכֶ֑ם וְעָמַ֣דְנוּ תַחְתֵּ֔ינוּ וְלֹ֥א נַעֲלֶ֖ה אֲלֵיהֶֽם׃

records.literal_gloss: If thus they say to us, Be still until we reach you, then we will stand in our place and not we will go up to them.

en.L: If they say thus to us, 'Be still until we reach you,' then we will stand in our place and will not go up to them.
en.B: If they say to us, 'Stay where you are until we come to you,' then we will stand where we are and not go up to them.
en.R: If they say to us, 'Wait there until we come to you,' then we will not move. We will not go up to them.

decisions.choice: be still: stop and stay where you are
decisions.reason: The verb means to be silent or motionless. The Philistines would be telling the two to halt while they come to deal with them.

decisions.choice: the first half of a sign: if this happens, they will not attack
decisions.reason: Jonathan sets two possible answers side by side. This one would mean that they should stay where they are; the second (verse 10) would mean that Yahweh is giving them victory.

source.text: וְאִם־כֹּ֨ה יֹאמְר֜וּ עֲל֤וּ עָלֵ֨ינוּ֙ וְעָלִ֔ינוּ כִּֽי־נְתָנָ֥ם יְהוָ֖ה בְּיָדֵ֑נוּ וְזֶה־לָּ֖נוּ הָאֽוֹת׃

records.literal_gloss: And if thus they say, Come up to us, then we will go up, for has given them Yahweh into our hand; and this to us [is] the sign.

en.L: But if they say thus, 'Come up to us,' then we will go up, for {{divine_name:the LORD|Yahweh}} has given them into our hand; and this [will be] the sign for us."
en.B: But if they say, 'Come up to us,' then we will go up, because {{divine_name:the LORD|Yahweh}} has given them into our power. That will be our sign."
en.R: But if they say, 'Come up here to us,' then we will go up. That will be our sign that {{divine_name:the LORD|Yahweh}} has handed them over to us."

decisions.choice: the sign: an agreed event by which to know Yahweh's will
decisions.reason: Asking for a sign before acting is found elsewhere in these books (Genesis 24:14; Judges 6:36-40). Here the enemy's own words will give the answer.

decisions.choice: given them into our hand: put them in our power
decisions.reason: "Hand" stands for power and control. The verb is in the completed form: if the sign comes, the victory is already settled.

decisions.choice: come up: a sign that runs against military sense
decisions.reason: Climbing up to an enemy who holds the heights is the more dangerous choice. Jonathan makes the risky answer the sign of Yahweh's help, so that the victory will clearly be Yahweh's.

decisions.choice: That will be our sign that the LORD has handed them over to us
decisions.reason: Readable joins the reason and the sign into one sentence; the meaning is the same.

source.text: וַיִּגָּל֣וּ שְׁנֵיהֶ֔ם אֶל־מַצַּ֖ב פְּלִשְׁתִּ֑ים וַיֹּאמְר֣וּ פְלִשְׁתִּ֔ים הִנֵּ֤ה עִבְרִים֙ יֹֽצְאִ֔ים מִן־הַחֹרִ֖ים אֲשֶׁ֥ר הִתְחַבְּאוּ־שָֽׁם׃

records.literal_gloss: And revealed themselves both of them to [the] garrison of [the] Philistines, and said [the] Philistines, Look, Hebrews coming out from the holes where they have hidden themselves there.

en.L: And both of them showed themselves to the garrison of the Philistines, and the Philistines said, "Look, Hebrews [are] coming out of the holes where they have hidden themselves."
en.B: So the two of them let the Philistine outpost see them. And the Philistines said, "Look! Hebrews are coming out of the holes where they have been hiding."
en.R: So the two of them came out where the Philistines at the outpost could see them. The Philistines said, "Look! The Hebrews are coming out of the holes they were hiding in!"

decisions.choice: Hebrews: the name others used for Israelites
decisions.reason: In 1 Samuel the Philistines call the Israelites "Hebrews", often with contempt (4:6, 9; 13:19; 29:3).

decisions.choice: the holes where they have hidden: the hiding places of 13:6
decisions.reason: When the Philistines gathered, the Israelites hid in caves, thickets, rocks, pits and cisterns (13:6). The soldiers mock them as creatures coming out of their burrows.

decisions.choice: are coming out
decisions.reason: English supplies the verb "are" that the Hebrew participle leaves out.

source.text: וַיַּעֲנוּ֩ אַנְשֵׁ֨י הַמַּצָּבָ֜ה אֶת־יוֹנָתָ֣ן׀וְאֶת־נֹשֵׂ֣א כֵלָ֗יו וַיֹּֽאמְרוּ֙ עֲל֣וּ אֵלֵ֔ינוּ וְנוֹדִ֥יעָה אֶתְכֶ֖ם דָּבָ֑רפוַיֹּ֨אמֶר יוֹנָתָ֜ן אֶל־נֹשֵׂ֤א כֵלָיו֙ עֲלֵ֣ה אַחֲרַ֔י כִּֽי־נְתָנָ֥ם יְהוָ֖ה בְּיַ֥ד יִשְׂרָאֵֽל׃

records.literal_gloss: And answered [the] men of the garrison Jonathan and his armor-bearer and said, Come up to us, and we will make known to you a thing. And said Jonathan to his armor-bearer, Come up after me, for has given them Yahweh into [the] hand of Israel.

en.L: And the men of the garrison answered Jonathan and his armor-bearer and said, "Come up to us, and we will make something known to you." And Jonathan said to his armor-bearer, "Come up after me, for {{divine_name:the LORD|Yahweh}} has given them into the hand of Israel."
en.B: The men at the outpost shouted to Jonathan and his armor-bearer, "Come up here to us, and we will teach you a lesson!" Jonathan said to his armor-bearer, "Climb up behind me, for {{divine_name:the LORD|Yahweh}} has given them into Israel's power."
en.R: The men at the outpost shouted to Jonathan and the young man, "Come up here, and we will teach you a lesson!" So Jonathan told the young man, "Follow me up. {{divine_name:the LORD|Yahweh}} has handed them over to Israel!"

decisions.choice: we will make known to you a thing: a mocking threat
decisions.reason: The words sound like an offer to tell them something, but in the soldiers' mouths they mean "we will show you" or "we will teach you a lesson".

decisions.choice: come up: the sign Jonathan had named is given
decisions.reason: The soldiers say the very words of verse 10. Jonathan takes them as Yahweh's answer and speaks of the victory as already given, and given to Israel, not only to the two of them.

decisions.choice: we will teach you a lesson
decisions.reason: The idiom carries the soldiers' scorn better than "make something known". Literal keeps the Hebrew wording.

source.text: וַיַּ֣עַל יוֹנָתָ֗ן עַל־יָדָיו֙ וְעַל־רַגְלָ֔יו וְנֹשֵׂ֥א כֵלָ֖יו אַחֲרָ֑יו וַֽיִּפְּלוּ֙ לִפְנֵ֣י יוֹנָתָ֔ן וְנֹשֵׂ֥א כֵלָ֖יו מְמוֹתֵ֥ת אַחֲרָֽיו׃

records.literal_gloss: And climbed Jonathan on his hands and on his feet, and his armor-bearer after him; and they fell before Jonathan, and his armor-bearer [was] killing after him.

en.L: And Jonathan climbed up on his hands and on his feet, and his armor-bearer after him. And they fell before Jonathan, and his armor-bearer [was] putting [them] to death behind him.
en.B: Jonathan climbed up using his hands and feet, and his armor-bearer followed. The Philistines fell before Jonathan, and his armor-bearer, coming after him, finished them off.
en.R: Jonathan climbed up the cliff on his hands and feet, and the young man climbed behind him. Jonathan struck the Philistines down, and the young man came behind him and killed them.

decisions.choice: on his hands and on his feet: scrambling up the rock
decisions.reason: The crag was too steep to walk up (verses 4-5). Jonathan climbs on all fours, which also means he comes up where no guard expects an attack.

decisions.choice: they fell before Jonathan: the Philistines went down under his blows
decisions.reason: The subject is the men of the garrison. Jonathan strikes them down, and the armor-bearer follows behind him.

decisions.choice: killing behind him: finishing off those Jonathan had struck down
decisions.reason: The form of the verb means "to put to death" and is used of making sure a wounded man dies (17:51; 2 Samuel 1:9-10). The two men work together: one fells, the other kills.

decisions.choice: The Philistines
decisions.reason: Balanced and Readable name the subject, which the Hebrew leaves to be understood from verse 12.

source.text: וַתְּהִ֞י הַמַּכָּ֣ה הָרִאשֹׁנָ֗ה אֲשֶׁ֨ר הִכָּ֧ה יוֹנָתָ֛ן וְנֹשֵׂ֥א כֵלָ֖יו כְּעֶשְׂרִ֣ים אִ֑ישׁ כְּבַחֲצִ֥י מַעֲנָ֖ה צֶ֥מֶד שָׂדֶֽה׃

records.literal_gloss: And was the slaughter the first which struck Jonathan and his armor-bearer about twenty man, within about half a furrow, [a] yoke of field.

en.L: And the first slaughter that Jonathan and his armor-bearer made was about twenty men, within about half a furrow of a yoke of field.
en.B: In that first attack Jonathan and his armor-bearer killed about twenty men within an area of about {{units:half an acre|half a furrow of a yoke of land}}.
en.R: In that first attack Jonathan and the young man killed about twenty men, in a space of about {{units:half an acre|half a furrow of a yoke of land}}.

decisions.choice: half a furrow of a yoke of field: a small piece of ground, perhaps half an acre
alternatives: about half the length of a furrow in a plowed field
decisions.reason: A "yoke" of land was the area a pair of oxen could plow in a day (Isaiah 5:10), and a furrow is the length of one plowed line. How the two words fit together here is not clear, and the exact size cannot be known. The point is that twenty men fell in a very small space, all at once.

decisions.choice: the first slaughter: the opening blow of the whole battle
decisions.reason: "First" marks this as the start: the panic and the rout of verses 15-23 follow from it.

decisions.choice: half an acre, with the Hebrew measure as the alternative
decisions.reason: Balanced and Readable give a modern equivalent with the original measure in the units setting. Literal keeps the Hebrew words.

source.text: וַתְּהִי֩ חֲרָדָ֨ה בַמַּחֲנֶ֤ה בַשָּׂדֶה֙ וּבְכָל־הָעָ֔ם הַמַּצָּב֙ וְהַמַּשְׁחִ֔ית חָרְד֖וּ גַּם־הֵ֑מָּה וַתִּרְגַּ֣ז הָאָ֔רֶץ וַתְּהִ֖י לְחֶרְדַּ֥ת אֱלֹהִֽים׃

records.literal_gloss: And was trembling in the camp, in the field and among all the people; the garrison and the raiders trembled, also they; and quaked the earth, and it became a trembling of God.

en.L: And there was trembling in the camp, in the field, and among all the people; the garrison and the raiders, they too trembled. And the earth quaked, and it became a trembling of God.
en.B: Panic struck the camp, the open country and all the troops. Even the outpost and the raiding parties trembled. The ground shook, and it became a panic sent by God.
en.R: Terror spread through the whole Philistine army, in the camp and out in the fields. Even the soldiers at the outpost and the raiding groups shook with fear. Then the ground shook, and the terror that God sent was everywhere.

decisions.choice: a trembling of God: a panic sent by God
decisions.reason: The phrase can mean a terror that comes from God, as when Yahweh threw enemies into panic before Israel (Exodus 23:27; Deuteronomy 7:23; 1 Samuel 7:10). Hebrew can also use "of God" to mean "very great", so it may be simply "an enormous panic". The earthquake in the same sentence points to God at work, so the first sense is preferred.

decisions.choice: the raiders: the raiding companies of 13:17-18
decisions.reason: The Philistines had sent out three raiding bands from their camp to plunder the land. Even these troops, away from the camp, are caught up in the panic.

decisions.choice: all the people: the whole Philistine army
decisions.reason: Here "the people" are the Philistine troops, in the camp and spread out in the open country.

decisions.choice: the whole Philistine army
decisions.reason: Readable names the army that "all the people" refers to.

source.text: וַיִּרְא֤וּ הַצֹּפִים֙ לְשָׁא֔וּל בְּגִבְעַ֖ת בִּנְיָמִ֑ן וְהִנֵּ֧ה הֶהָמ֛וֹן נָמ֖וֹג וַיֵּ֥לֶךְ וַהֲלֹֽם׃פ

records.literal_gloss: And saw [the] watchmen of Saul in Gibeah of Benjamin, and look, the multitude melted, and it went and hither.

en.L: And Saul's watchmen in Gibeah of Benjamin looked, and there was the throng, melting away and going this way and that.
en.B: Saul's lookouts in Gibeah of Benjamin saw the crowd of soldiers melting away, scattering in every direction.
en.R: Saul's lookouts at Gibeah in Benjamin saw the huge Philistine army breaking up and running off in all directions.

decisions.choice: melted: lost courage and broke apart
decisions.reason: The verb is used of people whose courage dissolves in terror (Exodus 15:15; Joshua 2:9, 24). The great camp is coming apart.

decisions.choice: it went and hither: it moved this way and that
decisions.reason: The Hebrew is short and unusual, literally "and it went, and here". It is taken as a picture of a crowd running in every direction. The Greek translation reads "here and there", which gives the same sense.

decisions.choice: watchmen: lookouts posted on high ground
decisions.reason: From the heights by Gibeah the lookouts could see across the ravine to the Philistine camp at Michmash.

decisions.choice: the huge Philistine army
decisions.reason: Readable says whose "throng" it is.

source.text: וַיֹּ֣אמֶר שָׁא֗וּל לָעָם֙ אֲשֶׁ֣ר אִתּ֔וֹ פִּקְדוּ־נָ֣א וּרְא֔וּ מִ֖י הָלַ֣ךְ מֵעִמָּ֑נוּ וַֽיִּפְקְד֔וּ וְהִנֵּ֛ה אֵ֥ין יוֹנָתָ֖ן וְנֹשֵׂ֥א כֵלָֽיו׃

records.literal_gloss: And said Saul to the people who [were] with him, Muster please and see who has gone from with us. And they mustered, and look, not Jonathan and his armor-bearer.

en.L: And Saul said to the people who [were] with him, "Count, please, and see who has gone from us." And they counted, and look, Jonathan and his armor-bearer [were] not [there].
en.B: Saul said to the troops with him, "Count the men and see who is missing." When they counted, Jonathan and his armor-bearer were not there.
en.R: Saul said to his men, "Count everyone and find out who is missing." When they counted, they found that Jonathan and the young man who carried his armor were not there.

decisions.choice: muster: count and check the troops
decisions.reason: The verb is used of counting soldiers by name or by unit (11:8; 13:15). Saul guesses that someone from his own side has caused the uproar.

decisions.choice: look, not Jonathan: the discovery
decisions.reason: The word "look" brings the reader to the moment of finding out. Saul learns what the reader already knows (verse 1).

decisions.choice: Count the men
decisions.reason: Balanced says what the mustering consisted of, a count of the men present.

source.text: וַיֹּ֤אמֶר שָׁאוּל֙ לַֽאֲחִיָּ֔ה הַגִּ֖ישָׁה אֲר֣וֹן הָאֱלֹהִ֑ים כִּֽי־הָיָ֞ה אֲר֧וֹן הָאֱלֹהִ֛ים בַּיּ֥וֹם הַה֖וּא וּבְנֵ֥י יִשְׂרָאֵֽל׃

records.literal_gloss: And said Saul to Ahijah, Bring near [the] ark of God, for was [the] ark of God on the day that, and [the] sons of Israel.

en.L: And Saul said to Ahijah, "Bring the ark of God near." For the ark of God was on that day [with] the sons of Israel.
en.B: Saul said to Ahijah, "Bring the ark of God here." At that time the ark of God was with the Israelites.
en.R: Saul said to Ahijah, "Bring God's ark here." At that time the ark of God was with the Israelites.

decisions.choice: the ark of God, as the Hebrew text reads
alternatives: Bring the ephod, for he carried the ephod on that day before Israel
decisions.reason: The Hebrew text has "the ark of God" twice. The ancient Greek translation reads instead: "Bring the ephod, for he carried the ephod on that day before Israel." Several things favor the Greek: the ark had been left at Kiriath-jearim (7:1-2) and stays there until David brings it up (2 Samuel 6:2-3); Ahijah has just been described as wearing an ephod (verse 3); Saul's words "withdraw your hand" (verse 19) fit the drawing of an answer from the ephod; and later "bring the ephod" is the usual request when God is asked (23:9; 30:7). On the other side, the Hebrew is the harder reading, and the ark had been taken into battle before (4:3-4). The Hebrew text is kept here, with the Greek reading noted. This note describes the ancient translations from general knowledge; it must be checked against a critical apparatus before review.

decisions.choice: bring near: Saul means to ask God before acting
decisions.reason: Whether by the ark or by the ephod, Saul wants the priest to seek God's answer about the battle. He breaks off before it comes (verse 19).

decisions.choice: and the sons of Israel: with the Israelites
decisions.reason: The Hebrew joins the last words with a simple "and". It is read as "with the Israelites", that is, among the troops at that time.

decisions.choice: [with]
decisions.reason: Literal brackets the "with" that the bare "and" implies. The "sons of Israel" here are the soldiers, so no inclusive alternative is given.

source.text: וַיְהִ֗י עַ֣ד דִּבֶּ֤ר שָׁאוּל֙ אֶל־הַכֹּהֵ֔ן וְהֶהָמ֗וֹן אֲשֶׁר֙ בְּמַחֲנֵ֣ה פְלִשְׁתִּ֔ים וַיֵּ֥לֶךְ הָל֖וֹךְ וָרָ֑בפוַיֹּ֧אמֶר שָׁא֛וּל אֶל־הַכֹּהֵ֖ן אֱסֹ֥ף יָדֶֽךָ׃

records.literal_gloss: And it was, while spoke Saul to the priest, and the tumult which [was] in [the] camp of [the] Philistines went on, going and increasing. And said Saul to the priest, Withdraw your hand.

en.L: And it happened, while Saul was speaking to the priest, that the tumult that [was] in the camp of the Philistines went on increasing more and more. And Saul said to the priest, "Withdraw your hand."
en.B: While Saul was talking to the priest, the uproar in the Philistine camp kept growing louder and louder. So Saul said to the priest, "Hold back your hand."
en.R: While Saul was still talking to the priest, the noise in the Philistine camp grew louder and louder. So Saul told the priest, "Stop what you are doing."

decisions.choice: withdraw your hand: stop the inquiry
decisions.reason: The priest had begun to seek God's answer, perhaps reaching into the ephod for the lots. Saul tells him to stop, because there is no time to wait.

decisions.choice: went on, going and increasing: grew steadily louder
decisions.reason: The repeated verb describes a noise that kept on growing. The uproar itself seems to answer Saul's question.

decisions.choice: Saul does not wait for God's answer
decisions.reason: Saul began to ask God and then broke off. Later, when he does ask, God gives him no answer (verse 37). Jonathan, by contrast, waited for a sign before acting (verses 8-10).

decisions.choice: Stop what you are doing
decisions.reason: Readable gives the sense of the idiom; see m1.

source.text: וַיִּזָּעֵ֣ק שָׁא֗וּל וְכָל־הָעָם֙ אֲשֶׁ֣ר אִתּ֔וֹ וַיָּבֹ֖אוּ עַד־הַמִּלְחָמָ֑ה וְהִנֵּ֨ה הָיְתָ֜ה חֶ֤רֶב אִישׁ֙ בְּרֵעֵ֔הוּ מְהוּמָ֖ה גְּדוֹלָ֥ה מְאֹֽד׃

records.literal_gloss: And were called together Saul and all the people who [were] with him, and they came to the battle; and look, was [the] sword of each against his neighbor, a confusion great very.

en.L: And Saul and all the people who [were] with him were called together, and they came to the battle. And look, every man's sword was against his fellow, a very great confusion.
en.B: Then Saul and all the troops with him rallied and went into the battle. There they found every Philistine's sword turned against his comrade, in utter confusion.
en.R: Saul and all his men gathered and went into the battle. They found the Philistines totally confused, attacking each other with their swords.

decisions.choice: every man's sword against his fellow: the enemy destroys itself
decisions.reason: The same thing happened when Gideon's three hundred blew their trumpets: Yahweh set every Midianite's sword against his comrade (Judges 7:22).

decisions.choice: confusion: the panic God brings on an enemy
decisions.reason: The word is used of the turmoil Yahweh sends on Israel's enemies in holy war (Deuteronomy 7:23) and on the Philistines (5:9, 11).

decisions.choice: were called together: rallied at a call
decisions.reason: The form means that Saul and his men were summoned or called out together, probably by a shout or a trumpet signal.

decisions.choice: every Philistine's sword; the Philistines
decisions.reason: Balanced and Readable name the Philistines, whom the Hebrew means by "each man".

source.text: וְהָעִבְרִ֗ים הָי֤וּ לַפְּלִשְׁתִּים֙ כְּאֶתְמ֣וֹל שִׁלְשׁ֔וֹם אֲשֶׁ֨ר עָל֥וּ עִמָּ֛ם בַּֽמַּחֲנֶ֖ה סָבִ֑יב וְגַם־הֵ֗מָּה לִֽהְיוֹת֙ עִם־יִשְׂרָאֵ֔ל אֲשֶׁ֥ר עִם־שָׁא֖וּל וְיוֹנָתָֽן׃

records.literal_gloss: And the Hebrews [who] were to the Philistines as yesterday [and] the day before, who went up with them in the camp all around, also they [turned] to be with Israel who [was] with Saul and Jonathan.

en.L: And the Hebrews [who] had been with the Philistines as before, who had gone up with them into the camp from all around, they too [turned] to be with Israel that [was] with Saul and Jonathan.
en.B: The Hebrews who had been with the Philistines before, and had gone up with them into the camp from the country around, also turned to join the Israelites who were with Saul and Jonathan.
en.R: Some Hebrews had been serving the Philistines for a while and had gone with them into their camp. Now they changed sides and joined the Israelites who were with Saul and Jonathan.

decisions.choice: the Hebrews who had been with the Philistines: Israelites in Philistine service
decisions.reason: Some Israelites had served or fought for the Philistines, as David would later do (27:2; 29:3). The Philistines call them "Hebrews", and the narrator uses their word here.

decisions.choice: as yesterday and the day before: previously, for some time
decisions.reason: The phrase means "as had been the case before" (4:7; 10:11).

decisions.choice: all around, they too: they turned to join Israel
alternatives: who had gone up with them into the camp, they too turned
decisions.reason: The Hebrew has no verb before "to be with Israel". The Greek and other ancient translations read "they turned", and in Hebrew "they turned" is spelled almost like the word for "all around". Either way the sense is that these men changed sides. This note describes the ancient translations from general knowledge; it must be checked against a critical apparatus before review.

decisions.choice: changed sides
decisions.reason: Readable says plainly what joining Israel meant for men who had been with the Philistines.

source.text: וְכֹל֩ אִ֨ישׁ יִשְׂרָאֵ֜ל הַמִּֽתְחַבְּאִ֤ים בְּהַר־אֶפְרַ֨יִם֙ שָֽׁמְע֔וּ כִּֽי־נָ֖סוּ פְּלִשְׁתִּ֑ים וַֽיַּדְבְּק֥וּ גַם־הֵ֛מָּה אַחֲרֵיהֶ֖ם בַּמִּלְחָמָֽה׃

records.literal_gloss: And every man of Israel who had hidden themselves in [the] hill country of Ephraim heard that had fled [the] Philistines, and they followed hard, also they, after them in the battle.

en.L: And all the men of Israel who had hidden themselves in the hill country of Ephraim heard that the Philistines had fled, and they too followed hard after them in the battle.
en.B: All the Israelites who had hidden in the hill country of Ephraim heard that the Philistines had fled, and they too joined the battle and kept close on their heels.
en.R: Other Israelites had been hiding up in the hills of Ephraim. When the news reached them that the Philistines were running away, they came out and joined in chasing them.

decisions.choice: who had hidden themselves: the men who hid in 13:6
decisions.reason: Many Israelites had hidden when the Philistines gathered (13:6-7). Now they come out to share in the victory.

decisions.choice: followed hard: pursued closely, kept on the heels of the enemy
decisions.reason: The verb means to cling to. Used of pursuit, it pictures soldiers staying right behind a fleeing enemy (31:2; Judges 20:42).

decisions.choice: the hill country of Ephraim: the highlands north of Benjamin
decisions.reason: The battle moves north and west from Michmash toward the high ground of Ephraim, where many had fled.

decisions.choice: they came out
decisions.reason: Readable says what hearing the news led them to do; the Hebrew implies it.

source.text: וַיּ֧וֹשַׁע יְהוָ֛ה בַּיּ֥וֹם הַה֖וּא אֶת־יִשְׂרָאֵ֑ל וְהַ֨מִּלְחָמָ֔ה עָבְרָ֖ה אֶת־בֵּ֥ית אָֽוֶן׃

records.literal_gloss: And saved Yahweh on the day that Israel, and the battle passed over Beth-aven.

en.L: So {{divine_name:the LORD|Yahweh}} saved Israel on that day, and the battle passed beyond Beth-aven.
en.B: So {{divine_name:the LORD|Yahweh}} saved Israel on that day, and the fighting moved on past Beth-aven.
en.R: That day {{divine_name:the LORD|Yahweh}} rescued Israel. The fighting spread all the way past Beth-aven.

decisions.choice: Yahweh saved Israel: the victory is Yahweh's
decisions.reason: The narrator gives the credit to Yahweh, using the verb Jonathan used in verse 6: Yahweh can save by many or by few. The same words close the account of the crossing of the sea (Exodus 14:30).

decisions.choice: Beth-aven: a place near Bethel, west of Michmash
decisions.reason: The Philistines had camped at Michmash "east of Beth-aven" (13:5; compare Joshua 7:2). The battle rolled west past it, toward the coast.

decisions.choice: rescued
decisions.reason: Readable uses an everyday word for the rescue; Literal and Balanced keep "saved".

source.text: וְאִֽישׁ־יִשְׂרָאֵ֥ל נִגַּ֖שׂ בַּיּ֣וֹם הַה֑וּא וַיֹּאֶל֩ שָׁא֨וּל אֶת־הָעָ֜ם לֵאמֹ֗ר אָר֣וּר הָ֠אִישׁ אֲשֶׁר־יֹ֨אכַל לֶ֜חֶם עַד־הָעֶ֗רֶב וְנִקַּמְתִּי֙ מֵאֹ֣יְבַ֔י וְלֹֽא טָעַ֥ם כָּל־הָעָ֖ם לָֽחֶם׃ס

records.literal_gloss: And [the] men of Israel were hard pressed on the day that; and Saul made swear the people, saying, Cursed [is] the man who eats food until the evening, and I am avenged on my enemies. And not tasted all the people food.

en.L: And the men of Israel were hard pressed on that day, for Saul had put the people under oath, saying, "Cursed [be] the man who eats food until the evening and I have taken vengeance on my enemies." So none of the people tasted food.
en.B: The Israelite troops were worn out that day, because Saul had bound the army with an oath: "Cursed be anyone who eats food before evening, before I have taken revenge on my enemies!" So none of the troops tasted any food.
en.R: The Israelite soldiers were in great distress that day. Saul had made them swear an oath. He said, "A curse will be on anyone who eats food before evening, before I have paid back my enemies!" So none of the soldiers ate anything.

decisions.choice: hard pressed: in distress, worn down
decisions.reason: The verb is used of people under heavy strain (13:6). Here the strain comes from their own king's oath: they must fight and pursue all day without food.

decisions.choice: made the people swear: put them under an oath with a curse
decisions.reason: Saul makes the troops share an oath with a curse attached to it. Anyone who breaks it falls under the curse, whether he knew of the oath or not, which is what happens to Jonathan (verses 27, 43).

decisions.choice: I am avenged on my enemies: Saul speaks of his own revenge
decisions.reason: The narrator has just said that Yahweh saved Israel (verse 23). Saul speaks of "my" enemies and "my" vengeance, and his oath weakens the people Yahweh is using.

decisions.choice: the men of Israel were hard pressed, as the Hebrew text reads
alternatives: Saul committed a great blunder that day
decisions.reason: The ancient Greek translation reads differently at the start of this verse, saying that Saul committed a great blunder that day, and it has a longer text around verses 23-24. The Hebrew text is followed. This note describes the ancient translations from general knowledge; it must be checked against a critical apparatus before review.

decisions.choice: anyone
decisions.reason: The curse applies to any soldier who eats, so Balanced and Readable say "anyone" for "the man".

source.text: וְכָל־הָאָ֖רֶץ בָּ֣אוּ בַיָּ֑עַר וַיְהִ֥י דְבַ֖שׁ עַל־פְּנֵ֥י הַשָּׂדֶֽה׃

records.literal_gloss: And all the land came into the forest, and there was honey on [the] face of the field.

en.L: And all the land came into the forest, and there was honey on the face of the ground.
en.B: The whole army came into the woods, and there was honey on the ground.
en.R: All the soldiers went into the woods, and there was honey lying on the ground.

decisions.choice: all the land: everyone in the land, here the whole army
alternatives: all the people of the land
decisions.reason: "The land" can stand for the people who live in it (2 Samuel 15:23). Here it means all the troops who were pursuing. The wording is unusual, and some think the text has suffered in copying, but the sense is clear from verse 26.

decisions.choice: honey: wild honey from bees' nests
decisions.reason: Wild bees nested in trees and in clefts of rock (Deuteronomy 32:13; Judges 14:8). Combs could break and drip honey onto the ground.

decisions.choice: the whole army; the woods
decisions.reason: Balanced and Readable say who "all the land" refers to. "Woods" fits a stand of trees in hill country better than "forest".

source.text: וַיָּבֹ֤א הָעָם֙ אֶל־הַיַּ֔עַר וְהִנֵּ֖ה הֵ֣לֶךְ דְּבָ֑שׁ וְאֵין־מַשִּׂ֤יג יָדוֹ֙ אֶל־פִּ֔יו כִּֽי־יָרֵ֥א הָעָ֖ם אֶת־הַשְּׁבֻעָֽה׃

records.literal_gloss: And came the people into the forest, and look, a flow of honey; and there was not [one] bringing his hand to his mouth, for feared the people the oath.

en.L: And the people came into the forest, and look, honey [was] flowing, but no one put his hand to his mouth, for the people feared the oath.
en.B: When the troops came into the woods, they saw honey dripping, yet no one lifted his hand to his mouth, because the troops were afraid of the oath.
en.R: When the soldiers came into the woods, they saw honey dripping down. But no one took any to eat. They were afraid because of the oath.

decisions.choice: a flow of honey: honey running from the combs
decisions.reason: The word means a going or flowing. The honey was there for the taking, which makes the soldiers' restraint the more striking.

decisions.choice: the people feared the oath: the oath had the force of a curse
decisions.reason: An oath made in God's name brought a curse on anyone who broke it (verse 24). The hungry soldiers would not risk it.

decisions.choice: no one took any to eat
decisions.reason: Readable gives the sense of "brought his hand to his mouth".

source.text: וְיוֹנָתָ֣ן לֹֽא־שָׁמַ֗ע בְּהַשְׁבִּ֣יעַ אָבִיו֮ אֶת־הָעָם֒ וַיִּשְׁלַ֗ח אֶת־קְצֵ֤ה הַמַּטֶּה֙ אֲשֶׁ֣ר בְּיָד֔וֹ וַיִּטְבֹּ֥ל אוֹתָ֖הּ בְּיַעְרַ֣ת הַדְּבָ֑שׁ וַיָּ֤שֶׁב יָדוֹ֙ אֶל־פִּ֔יו וַתָּאֹ֖רְנָה עֵינָֽיו׃

records.literal_gloss: And Jonathan not had heard when made swear his father the people, and he stretched out [the] end of the staff which [was] in his hand and dipped it in [the] comb of the honey, and brought back his hand to his mouth; and brightened his eyes.

en.L: But Jonathan had not heard when his father put the people under oath, and he stretched out the end of the staff that [was] in his hand and dipped it into the honeycomb, and brought his hand back to his mouth; and his eyes brightened.
en.B: But Jonathan had not heard his father put the army under oath. He reached out with the staff he was holding, dipped its tip into the honeycomb and raised it to his mouth, and his eyes brightened.
en.R: But Jonathan had not heard his father make the soldiers swear the oath. So he reached out the stick he was holding and dipped the end of it into a honeycomb. He put the honey into his mouth, and his eyes became bright. He felt strong again.

decisions.choice: his eyes brightened: his strength came back
decisions.reason: Dull eyes are a sign of exhaustion, and bright eyes of renewed life and strength (Psalm 13:4; Ezra 9:8). The honey revived him at once.

decisions.choice: brightened, as the Hebrew is read aloud
decisions.reason: The consonants written in the text can be read "and his eyes saw"; the scribes' marginal reading, followed here, is "and his eyes brightened", as in verse 29. The two words differ only in the order of two letters.

decisions.choice: Jonathan had not heard: he was away when the oath was made
decisions.reason: Jonathan had left the camp without telling anyone (verse 1), so he knew nothing of the oath. The story turns on this: he breaks an oath he never heard.

decisions.choice: He felt strong again
decisions.reason: Readable says what bright eyes meant; see m1.

source.text: וַיַּעַן֩ אִ֨ישׁ מֵֽהָעָ֜ם וַיֹּ֗אמֶר הַשְׁבֵּעַ֩ הִשְׁבִּ֨יעַ אָבִ֤יךָ אֶת־הָעָם֙ לֵאמֹ֔ר אָר֥וּר הָאִ֛ישׁ אֲשֶׁר־יֹ֥אכַל לֶ֖חֶם הַיּ֑וֹם וַיָּ֖עַף הָעָֽם׃

records.literal_gloss: And answered a man of the people and said, Surely made swear your father the people, saying, Cursed [is] the man who eats food today. And was faint the people.

en.L: And a man of the people answered and said, "Your father strictly put the people under oath, saying, 'Cursed [be] the man who eats food today.' And the people are faint."
en.B: One of the soldiers told him, "Your father made the troops swear a solemn oath: 'Cursed be anyone who eats food today.' That is why the troops are exhausted."
en.R: One of the soldiers said to him, "Your father made all of us swear an oath. He said, 'A curse will be on anyone who eats food today!' That is why everyone is so tired and weak."

decisions.choice: surely made swear: a strict, solemn oath
decisions.reason: The verb is doubled for emphasis. The soldier stresses how binding the oath was.

decisions.choice: and the people are faint: the soldier's words
alternatives: the narrator says: and the people were faint
decisions.reason: The last clause may belong to the soldier, explaining why the troops are so weak, or it may be the narrator's remark. Jonathan's answer in verses 29-30 picks up the people's weakness, which suits the soldier saying it.

decisions.choice: today: the oath as the soldier reports it
decisions.reason: Saul's words in verse 24 were "until evening". The soldier gives their effect for that day.

decisions.choice: anyone
decisions.reason: As in verse 24.

source.text: וַיֹּ֨אמֶר֙ יֽוֹנָתָ֔ן עָכַ֥ר אָבִ֖י אֶת־הָאָ֑רֶץ רְאוּ־נָא֙ כִּֽי־אֹ֣רוּ עֵינַ֔י כִּ֣י טָעַ֔מְתִּי מְעַ֖ט דְּבַ֥שׁ הַזֶּֽה׃

records.literal_gloss: And said Jonathan, Has troubled my father the land; see please that have brightened my eyes, because I tasted a little of honey the this.

en.L: And Jonathan said, "My father has troubled the land. See, please, how my eyes have brightened because I tasted a little of this honey.
en.B: Jonathan said, "My father has brought trouble on the land. See how my eyes have brightened since I tasted this bit of honey.
en.R: Jonathan said, "My father has made trouble for the whole country. See how much better I feel! My eyes are bright because I tasted a little of this honey.

decisions.choice: troubled: the word used of Achan, who brought disaster on Israel
decisions.reason: Achan was called the one who "troubled Israel", and the valley of his judgment was named Achor, "trouble" (Joshua 7:25-26). Jonathan uses the same strong word of his father. The irony is that the lot will soon fall on Jonathan himself.

decisions.choice: my eyes have brightened: I have my strength back
decisions.reason: See verse 27.

decisions.choice: See how much better I feel!
decisions.reason: Readable spells out what Jonathan asks them to see; see verse 27.

source.text: אַ֗ף כִּ֡י לוּא֩ אָכֹ֨ל אָכַ֤ל הַיּוֹם֙ הָעָ֔ם מִשְּׁלַ֥ל אֹיְבָ֖יו אֲשֶׁ֣ר מָצָ֑א כִּ֥י עַתָּ֛ה לֹֽא־רָבְתָ֥ה מַכָּ֖ה בַּפְּלִשְׁתִּֽים׃

records.literal_gloss: How much more if surely had eaten today the people from [the] plunder of its enemies which it found! For now not has been great [the] slaughter among [the] Philistines.

en.L: How much more if the people had eaten freely today from the plunder of their enemies that they found! For now the slaughter among the Philistines has not been great."
en.B: How much better if the troops had eaten freely today from what they took from their enemies as plunder! As it is, the defeat of the Philistines has not been great."
en.R: If only the soldiers had eaten today some of the food they took from their enemies! Then we would have killed many more Philistines than we have."

decisions.choice: how much more if: a wish about what did not happen
decisions.reason: Jonathan argues from the lesser to the greater: if a little honey revived him, food for the whole army would have done far more. The doubled verb means "eaten freely".

decisions.choice: for now the slaughter has not been great: as things are, the victory is smaller than it could have been
alternatives: for then would not the slaughter among the Philistines have been greater?
decisions.reason: The clause can be read as a statement or as a question, "would not the slaughter have been greater?" Both say that the oath has cost Israel part of its victory.

decisions.choice: plunder: goods and livestock taken from the enemy
decisions.reason: The plunder included the flocks and herds the troops later fall upon (verse 32).

decisions.choice: Then we would have killed many more Philistines than we have
decisions.reason: Readable states as a plain result what the Hebrew gives as a contrast with "now".

source.text: וַיַּכּ֞וּ בַּיּ֤וֹם הַהוּא֙ בַּפְּלִשְׁתִּ֔ים מִמִּכְמָ֖שׂ אַיָּלֹ֑נָה וַיָּ֥עַף הָעָ֖ם מְאֹֽד׃

records.literal_gloss: And they struck on the day that among [the] Philistines from Michmash to Aijalon, and was faint the people very.

en.L: And on that day they struck down [men] among the Philistines from Michmash to Aijalon, and the people were very faint.
en.B: That day the Israelites struck down the Philistines all the way from Michmash to Aijalon, and the troops were utterly exhausted.
en.R: That day the Israelites kept attacking the Philistines all the way from Michmash to Aijalon. By then the soldiers were completely worn out.

decisions.choice: from Michmash to Aijalon: a long pursuit westward
decisions.reason: Aijalon lies far to the west of Michmash, where the hill country drops toward the coastal plain (Joshua 10:12). The Philistines were fleeing home toward their own cities.

decisions.choice: struck among the Philistines: killed many of them
decisions.reason: The phrase means that they cut down Philistines along the way, not that the whole army was destroyed.

decisions.choice: the people were very faint: the result of the oath
decisions.reason: After a long day of pursuit without food, the troops are at the end of their strength. This explains what they do next (verse 32).

decisions.choice: the Israelites
decisions.reason: Balanced and Readable name the subject of "they struck".

source.text: וַיַּ֤עַט הָעָם֙ אֶל־הַשָּׁלָ֔ל וַיִּקְח֨וּ צֹ֧אן וּבָקָ֛ר וּבְנֵ֥י בָקָ֖ר וַיִּשְׁחֲטוּ־אָ֑רְצָה וַיֹּ֥אכַל הָעָ֖ם עַל־הַדָּֽם׃

records.literal_gloss: And rushed the people on the plunder, and they took sheep and cattle and sons of cattle, and slaughtered [them] on the ground, and ate the people with the blood.

en.L: And the people rushed on the plunder, and they took sheep and cattle and calves and slaughtered [them] on the ground, and the people ate [them] with the blood.
en.B: The troops pounced on the plunder. They took sheep, cattle and calves, slaughtered them on the ground, and ate them with the blood still in them.
en.R: The soldiers grabbed the animals they had taken from the enemy: sheep, cattle and calves. They killed them right there on the ground and ate the meat with the blood still in it.

decisions.choice: rushed on the plunder, as the Hebrew is read aloud
alternatives: and the people made for plunder
decisions.reason: The consonants written in the text read "and the people made for plunder"; the scribes' marginal reading, followed here, is "and the people rushed on the plunder". The verb pictures a bird of prey swooping down, as in 15:19.

decisions.choice: with the blood: against the law forbidding blood
decisions.reason: The law forbade eating meat with its blood, because the life is in the blood (Genesis 9:4; Leviticus 17:10-14; 19:26; Deuteronomy 12:16, 23-24). The blood had to be drained out and poured on the ground before the meat was eaten.

decisions.choice: on the ground: killed where they stood, without draining the blood
decisions.reason: Animals slaughtered flat on the ground could not be properly bled before they were eaten. Saul's large stone (verses 33-34) solves this.

decisions.choice: the animals they had taken from the enemy
decisions.reason: Readable says what the plunder was, which the list that follows makes clear.

source.text: וַיַּגִּ֤ידוּ לְשָׁאוּל֙ לֵאמֹ֔ר הִנֵּ֥ה הָעָ֛ם חֹטִ֥אים לַֽיהוָ֖ה לֶאֱכֹ֣ל עַל־הַדָּ֑ם וַיֹּ֣אמֶר בְּגַדְתֶּ֔ם גֹּֽלּוּ־אֵלַ֥י הַיּ֖וֹם אֶ֥בֶן גְּדוֹלָֽה׃

records.literal_gloss: And they told Saul, saying, Look, the people [are] sinning against Yahweh by eating with the blood. And he said, You have dealt faithlessly; roll to me today a stone great.

en.L: And they told Saul, saying, "Look, the people are sinning against {{divine_name:the LORD|Yahweh}} by eating with the blood." And he said, "You have acted faithlessly. Roll a great stone to me today."
en.B: Saul was told, "Look, the troops are sinning against {{divine_name:the LORD|Yahweh}}. They are eating meat with the blood in it." He said, "You have broken faith! Roll a large stone over to me at once."
en.R: Someone told Saul, "Look! The soldiers are sinning against {{divine_name:the LORD|Yahweh}}. They are eating meat with the blood still in it." Saul said, "You have been unfaithful! Roll a big stone over here to me right now."

decisions.choice: you have dealt faithlessly: you have broken faith
decisions.reason: The verb is used of betraying a trust or a covenant. Saul accuses the troops of breaking faith with Yahweh, though it was his own oath that drove them to it.

decisions.choice: a great stone: a place to slaughter the animals properly
decisions.reason: Killed on a raised stone, the animals could be bled, and the blood would run off onto the ground before the meat was eaten (Deuteronomy 12:16).

decisions.choice: today: now, at once
alternatives: roll a great stone to me here
decisions.reason: "Today" here means "right now". The Greek translation reads "here", which in Hebrew is a similar word; the sense is much the same. This note describes the ancient translations from general knowledge; it must be checked against a critical apparatus before review.

decisions.choice: eating meat with the blood in it
decisions.reason: Balanced and Readable supply "meat" and say what eating "with the blood" means.

source.text: וַיֹּ֣אמֶר שָׁא֣וּל פֻּ֣צוּ בָעָ֡ם וַאֲמַרְתֶּ֣ם לָהֶ֡ם הַגִּ֣ישׁוּ אֵלַי֩ אִ֨ישׁ שׁוֹר֜וֹ וְאִ֣ישׁ שְׂיֵ֗הוּ וּשְׁחַטְתֶּ֤ם בָּזֶה֙ וַאֲכַלְתֶּ֔ם וְלֹֽא־תֶחֶטְא֥וּ לַֽיהוָ֖ה לֶאֱכֹ֣ל אֶל־הַדָּ֑ם וַיַּגִּ֨שׁוּ כָל־הָעָ֜ם אִ֣ישׁ שׁוֹר֧וֹ בְיָד֛וֹ הַלַּ֖יְלָה וַיִּשְׁחֲטוּ־שָֽׁם׃

records.literal_gloss: And said Saul, Scatter among the people and say to them, Bring near to me each his ox and each his sheep, and slaughter in this and eat, and not sin against Yahweh by eating with the blood. And brought near all the people each his ox in his hand the night, and they slaughtered there.

en.L: And Saul said, "Scatter among the people and say to them, 'Bring to me each man his ox and each man his sheep, and slaughter [them] on this and eat; and do not sin against {{divine_name:the LORD|Yahweh}} by eating with the blood.'" And all the people brought each man his ox with him that night, and they slaughtered [them] there.
en.B: Then Saul said, "Go out among the troops and tell them, 'Each of you bring me your ox or your sheep. Slaughter them here and eat. Do not sin against {{divine_name:the LORD|Yahweh}} by eating meat that still has its blood.'" So that night all the troops brought their oxen with them and slaughtered them there.
en.R: Then Saul said, "Go out among the soldiers and tell them this: 'Every man must bring his ox or his sheep to me and kill it here. Then you may eat. Do not sin against {{divine_name:the LORD|Yahweh}} by eating meat that still has blood in it.'" That night each soldier brought his ox, and they killed the animals there.

decisions.choice: in this: on this stone
decisions.reason: "This" is the great stone of verse 33. Slaughtering on it let the blood drain away as the law required.

decisions.choice: in his hand: with him, himself
decisions.reason: Each man brought his own animal, leading it by hand.

decisions.choice: his ox and his sheep: whatever animal each one had taken
decisions.reason: The list means each man's share of the captured animals, an ox or a sheep.

decisions.choice: your ox or your sheep; his ox or his sheep
decisions.reason: Balanced and Readable say "or", since each man brought one animal.

source.text: וַיִּ֧בֶן שָׁא֛וּל מִזְבֵּ֖חַ לַֽיהוָ֑ה אֹת֣וֹ הֵחֵ֔ל לִבְנ֥וֹת מִזְבֵּ֖חַ לַֽיהוָֽה׃פ

records.literal_gloss: And built Saul an altar to Yahweh; it he began to build [as an] altar to Yahweh.

en.L: And Saul built an altar to {{divine_name:the LORD|Yahweh}}; it [was the first] he began to build as an altar to {{divine_name:the LORD|Yahweh}}.
en.B: Saul built an altar to {{divine_name:the LORD|Yahweh}}. It was the first altar he built to {{divine_name:the LORD|Yahweh}}.
en.R: Saul built an altar there to {{divine_name:the LORD|Yahweh}}. It was the first altar he ever built to {{divine_name:the LORD|Yahweh}}.

decisions.choice: it he began to build: it was the first altar Saul built
alternatives: he began building it as an altar to Yahweh
decisions.reason: The Hebrew says "it he began to build as an altar". This is taken to mean that it was the first altar Saul built. It could also mean that he began to build it, as if he left it unfinished when he turned to the night pursuit (verse 36).

decisions.choice: an altar: perhaps built around the great stone
decisions.reason: The stone where the animals were slaughtered (verse 33) may have become part of the altar, so that the meal was set right before Yahweh.

decisions.choice: [was the first]
decisions.reason: Literal brackets the words that the verb "began" implies.

source.text: וַיֹּ֣אמֶר שָׁא֡וּל נֵרְדָ֣ה אַחֲרֵי֩ פְלִשְׁתִּ֨ים׀לַ֜יְלָה וְֽנָבֹ֥זָה בָהֶ֣ם׀עַד־א֣וֹר הַבֹּ֗קֶר וְלֹֽא־נַשְׁאֵ֤ר בָּהֶם֙ אִ֔ישׁ וַיֹּ֣אמְר֔וּ כָּל־הַטּ֥וֹב בְּעֵינֶ֖יךָ עֲשֵׂ֑הסוַיֹּ֨אמֶר֙ הַכֹּהֵ֔ן נִקְרְבָ֥ה הֲלֹ֖ם אֶל־הָאֱלֹהִֽים׃

records.literal_gloss: And said Saul, Let us go down after [the] Philistines by night, and let us plunder among them until [the] light of the morning, and not let us leave among them a man. And they said, All the good in your eyes, do. And said the priest, Let us draw near here to God.

en.L: And Saul said, "Let us go down after the Philistines by night and plunder them until the light of the morning, and let us not leave a man among them." And they said, "Do all that [is] good in your eyes." And the priest said, "Let us draw near here to God."
en.B: Saul said, "Let us go down after the Philistines tonight and plunder them until daybreak. Let us not leave a single one of them alive." They answered, "Do whatever you think best." But the priest said, "Let us come near to God here first."
en.R: Then Saul said, "Let us go down and chase the Philistines tonight. We can take everything they have until morning comes, and we will not leave any of them alive." The men answered, "Do whatever you think is best." But the priest said, "First let us ask God about it."

decisions.choice: all the good in your eyes: whatever you think best
decisions.reason: The troops leave the decision to Saul. "In your eyes" means "in your judgment".

decisions.choice: let us draw near to God: let us ask God through the priest
decisions.reason: To come near to God here means to seek his answer by the priest's means of asking, as Saul began to do in verses 18-19. The priest will not let Saul act without it.

decisions.choice: let us not leave a man among them: let us wipe them out
decisions.reason: Saul wants to complete the victory before the Philistines can regroup.

decisions.choice: first
decisions.reason: Balanced and Readable add "first" to show that the priest is asking for an inquiry before the attack, which the context implies. Readable also says "ask God" for "draw near to God".

source.text: וַיִּשְׁאַ֤ל שָׁאוּל֙ בֵּֽאלֹהִ֔ים הַֽאֵרֵד֙ אַחֲרֵ֣י פְלִשְׁתִּ֔ים הֲתִתְּנֵ֖ם בְּיַ֣ד יִשְׂרָאֵ֑ל וְלֹ֥א עָנָ֖הוּ בַּיּ֥וֹם הַהֽוּא׃

records.literal_gloss: And asked Saul of God, Shall I go down after [the] Philistines? Will you give them into [the] hand of Israel? And not he answered him on the day that.

en.L: And Saul asked of God, "Shall I go down after the Philistines? Will {{deity_pronoun:you|You}} give them into the hand of Israel?" But {{deity_pronoun:he|He}} did not answer him on that day.
en.B: So Saul asked God, "Should I go down after the Philistines? Will {{deity_pronoun:you|You}} hand them over to Israel?" But God did not answer him that day.
en.R: So Saul asked God, "Should I go after the Philistines? Will {{deity_pronoun:you|You}} let Israel defeat them?" But God gave him no answer that day.

decisions.choice: Saul asked of God: an inquiry through the priest
decisions.reason: To "ask of God" was to put a question to God by the priest's lots, which gave a yes or a no (Judges 1:1; 20:18, 23; 1 Samuel 23:2-4). Saul asks two questions that can be answered that way.

decisions.choice: he did not answer him: God's silence is a warning
decisions.reason: No answer at all was taken as a sign that something stood between the one asking and God (28:6). Saul concludes that there has been a sin (verse 38).

decisions.choice: God did not answer him
decisions.reason: Balanced and Readable name God instead of using "he", so that it is clear who did not answer.

source.text: וַיֹּ֣אמֶר שָׁא֔וּל גֹּ֣שֽׁוּ הֲלֹ֔ם כֹּ֖ל פִּנּ֣וֹת הָעָ֑ם וּדְע֣וּ וּרְא֔וּ בַּמָּ֗ה הָֽיְתָ֛ה הַחַטָּ֥את הַזֹּ֖את הַיּֽוֹם׃

records.literal_gloss: And said Saul, Draw near here, all [the] corners of the people, and know and see in what has been the sin the this today.

en.L: And Saul said, "Come near here, all [you] corners of the people, and know and see how this sin has happened today.
en.B: Then Saul said, "Come here, all you leaders of the troops, and find out how this sin was committed today.
en.R: Saul said, "All you leaders of the army, come here. We must find out what sin was done today.

decisions.choice: the corners of the people: the leaders
decisions.reason: A cornerstone holds a building together, and the word is used of the chief men who hold a people together (Judges 20:2; Isaiah 19:13).

decisions.choice: in what has the sin been: how, and by whom, the sin came about
decisions.reason: Saul takes God's silence as proof that someone has sinned, and he means to find out who.

decisions.choice: leaders
decisions.reason: Balanced and Readable give the sense of the picture; see m1.

source.text: כִּ֣י חַי־יְהוָ֗ה הַמּוֹשִׁ֨יעַ֙ אֶת־יִשְׂרָאֵ֔ל כִּ֧י אִם־יֶשְׁנ֛וֹ בְּיוֹנָתָ֥ן בְּנִ֖י כִּ֣י מ֣וֹת יָמ֑וּת וְאֵ֥ין עֹנֵ֖הוּ מִכָּל־הָעָֽם׃

records.literal_gloss: For [as] Yahweh lives, who saves Israel, even if it is in Jonathan my son, surely he will die. And there was not [one] answering him from all the people.

en.L: For [as] {{divine_name:the LORD|Yahweh}} lives, who saves Israel, even if it is in Jonathan my son, he will surely die." But there was no one from all the people who answered him.
en.B: As surely as {{divine_name:the LORD|Yahweh}} lives, who saves Israel, even if the guilt lies with my son Jonathan, he must die!" Yet no one among the troops answered him.
en.R: {{divine_name:the LORD|Yahweh}} is the one who saves Israel, and as surely as {{deity_pronoun:he|He}} lives, even if my own son Jonathan did this, he must die!" But none of the men said a word.

decisions.choice: as Yahweh lives: a solemn oath
decisions.reason: The speaker calls on the living God as witness and guarantee. Having sworn by Yahweh's life, Saul has bound himself to carry out what he says.

decisions.choice: who saves Israel: a title that turns back on Saul
decisions.reason: Saul calls Yahweh the one who saves Israel, the same verb as in verses 6 and 23. The troops will answer that Yahweh saved Israel that day through Jonathan (verse 45).

decisions.choice: if it is in Jonathan: if the sin lies with Jonathan
decisions.reason: "It" is the sin of verse 38. Saul names his own son as an example, not yet knowing that the lot will fall on him.

decisions.choice: no one answered: the troops keep silent
decisions.reason: At least one soldier knew what Jonathan had done (verse 28). The silence may be loyalty to Jonathan or fear of Saul's oath.

decisions.choice: the guilt lies with
decisions.reason: Balanced supplies "the guilt" for the bare "it".

source.text: וַיֹּ֣אמֶר אֶל־כָּל־יִשְׂרָאֵ֗ל אַתֶּם֙ תִּֽהְיוּ֙ לְעֵ֣בֶר אֶחָ֔ד וַֽאֲנִי֙ וְיוֹנָתָ֣ן בְּנִ֔י נִהְיֶ֖ה לְעֵ֣בֶר אֶחָ֑ד וַיֹּאמְר֤וּ הָעָם֙ אֶל־שָׁא֔וּל הַטּ֥וֹב בְּעֵינֶ֖יךָ עֲשֵֽׂה׃ס

records.literal_gloss: And he said to all Israel, You will be on one side, and I and Jonathan my son will be on one side. And said the people to Saul, The good in your eyes do.

en.L: And he said to all Israel, "You will be on one side, and I and Jonathan my son will be on the other side." And the people said to Saul, "Do what [is] good in your eyes."
en.B: Then he said to all Israel, "You stand on one side, and my son Jonathan and I will stand on the other." The troops told Saul, "Do whatever you think best."
en.R: Then Saul said to all the Israelites, "You stand on one side. My son Jonathan and I will stand on the other side." The men answered, "Do whatever you think is best."

decisions.choice: two sides: the first step of a choice by lot
decisions.reason: The lot narrowed the search step by step, group by group, until one person was taken, as with Achan (Joshua 7:14-18) and with Saul himself at Mizpah (10:20-21).

decisions.choice: the good in your eyes do: do what you think best
decisions.reason: The same words as in verse 36. Then the troops gave Saul a free hand eagerly; now they go along with him in silence.

decisions.choice: the other side
decisions.reason: Hebrew says "one side ... one side"; English says "one side ... the other".

source.text: וַיֹּ֣אמֶר שָׁא֗וּל אֶל־יְהוָ֛ה אֱלֹהֵ֥י יִשְׂרָאֵ֖ל הָ֣בָה תָמִ֑ים וַיִּלָּכֵ֧ד יוֹנָתָ֛ן וְשָׁא֖וּל וְהָעָ֥ם יָצָֽאוּ׃

records.literal_gloss: And said Saul to Yahweh, God of Israel, Give perfect. And was taken Jonathan and Saul, and the people went out.

en.L: And Saul said to {{divine_name:the LORD|Yahweh}}, the God of Israel, "Give what is right." And Jonathan and Saul were taken, and the people went free.
en.B: Then Saul said to {{divine_name:the LORD|Yahweh}}, the God of Israel, "Show the right answer." Jonathan and Saul were taken by the lot, and the troops were cleared.
en.R: Then Saul prayed to {{divine_name:the LORD|Yahweh}}, the God of Israel, "Show us the truth." The lot pointed to Jonathan and Saul, and the rest of the men were cleared.

decisions.choice: give what is right, as the Hebrew text reads
alternatives: Why have you not answered your servant today? If this guilt is in me or in Jonathan my son, give Urim; if it is in your people Israel, give Thummim
decisions.reason: The Hebrew text is short: "Give perfect", or "Show the truth". The ancient Greek translation has a longer prayer: "Why have you not answered your servant today? If this guilt is in me or in Jonathan my son, Lord God of Israel, give Urim; and if it is in your people Israel, give Thummim." The word read "perfect" has the same consonants as "Thummim", and the longer prayer may have dropped out of the Hebrew when a copyist's eye jumped from one "Israel" to the next. The longer text fits the two sides of verse 40 and the use of lots that follows. The Hebrew text is kept here, with the Greek reading noted. This note describes the ancient translations from general knowledge; it must be checked against a critical apparatus before review.

decisions.choice: the lot: Urim and Thummim, the priest's means of asking God
decisions.reason: The Urim and Thummim were kept in the high priest's breastpiece (Exodus 28:30) and were used to ask Yahweh's decision (Numbers 27:21; 1 Samuel 28:6). They seem to have given a choice between two answers, which fits the two sides of verse 40.

decisions.choice: was taken: was picked out by the lot
decisions.reason: The verb means to be caught or seized; with a lot, it means to be singled out (10:20-21; Joshua 7:16-18).

decisions.choice: the people went out: they went free, they were cleared
decisions.reason: To "go out" here is to come out of the inquiry free of guilt.

decisions.choice: Show the right answer (Balanced); Show us the truth (Readable)
decisions.reason: The single word "perfect" is a request for a true, complete answer; Balanced and Readable say so. Readable says Saul "prayed", since he speaks to Yahweh.

source.text: וַיֹּ֣אמֶר שָׁא֔וּל הַפִּ֕ילוּ בֵּינִ֕י וּבֵ֖ין יוֹנָתָ֣ן בְּנִ֑י וַיִּלָּכֵ֖ד יוֹנָתָֽן׃

records.literal_gloss: And said Saul, Cast between me and between Jonathan my son. And was taken Jonathan.

en.L: And Saul said, "Cast [the lot] between me and Jonathan my son." And Jonathan was taken.
en.B: Then Saul said, "Cast the lot to decide between me and Jonathan my son." And Jonathan was taken.
en.R: Saul said, "Now cast the lot to choose between me and my son Jonathan." The lot pointed to Jonathan.

decisions.choice: cast: make the lot fall
decisions.reason: The verb means "cause to fall", the action of throwing or drawing lots.

decisions.choice: the short Hebrew text
decisions.reason: The ancient Greek translation is longer here. It adds that Saul said, "Whomever the Lord takes by lot shall die," that the people protested, and that Saul overruled them before the lot was cast. The Hebrew text is followed. This note describes the ancient translations from general knowledge; it must be checked against a critical apparatus before review.

decisions.choice: the lot
decisions.reason: English supplies the object of "cast", which the Hebrew leaves out; Literal brackets it.

source.text: וַיֹּ֤אמֶר שָׁאוּל֙ אֶל־י֣וֹנָתָ֔ן הַגִּ֥ידָה לִּ֖י מֶ֣ה עָשִׂ֑יתָה וַיַּגֶּד־ל֣וֹ יוֹנָתָ֗ן וַיֹּאמֶר֩ טָעֹ֨ם טָעַ֜מְתִּי בִּקְצֵ֨ה הַמַּטֶּ֧ה אֲשֶׁר־בְּיָדִ֛י מְעַ֥ט דְּבַ֖שׁ הִנְנִ֥י אָמֽוּת׃

records.literal_gloss: And said Saul to Jonathan, Tell me what you have done. And told him Jonathan and said, Surely I tasted with [the] end of the staff which [was] in my hand a little honey. Here I [am]; I will die.

en.L: And Saul said to Jonathan, "Tell me what you have done." And Jonathan told him and said, "I did taste a little honey with the end of the staff that [was] in my hand. Here I am; I will die."
en.B: Saul said to Jonathan, "Tell me what you have done." So Jonathan told him, "I tasted a little honey on the end of the staff I was holding. Here I am. I am ready to die."
en.R: Saul said to Jonathan, "Tell me what you did." Jonathan told him, "I just tasted a little honey with the tip of the stick I was holding. Here I am. I am ready to die."

decisions.choice: tell me what you have done: the words spoken to Achan
decisions.reason: Joshua said the same to Achan when the lot fell on him (Joshua 7:19). Saul treats his son as a man who has brought trouble on Israel, the word Jonathan used of Saul (verse 29).

decisions.choice: I did taste a little honey: a plain admission
decisions.reason: The doubled verb stresses that he really did it, while "a little" shows how small the act was.

decisions.choice: here I am; I will die: acceptance of the sentence
alternatives: here I am: must I die for this?
decisions.reason: Jonathan may be saying that he is ready to die, or he may be protesting, "and for this I must die?" The first is followed; it fits his plain confession. Either way he does not resist his father.

decisions.choice: just
decisions.reason: Readable adds "just" to bring out the force of "a little".

source.text: וַיֹּ֣אמֶר שָׁא֔וּל כֹּֽה־יַעֲשֶׂ֥ה אֱלֹהִ֖ים וְכֹ֣ה יוֹסִ֑ף כִּֽי־מ֥וֹת תָּמ֖וּת יוֹנָתָֽן׃

records.literal_gloss: And said Saul, Thus may do God, and thus may he add; for surely you will die, Jonathan.

en.L: And Saul said, "Thus may God do, and thus may {{deity_pronoun:he|He}} add; for you will surely die, Jonathan."
en.B: Saul said, "May God deal with me ever so severely if you do not die, Jonathan!"
en.R: Saul said, "Jonathan, you must die! May God punish me terribly if you do not!"

decisions.choice: thus may God do and thus may he add: a self-curse
decisions.reason: The speaker calls on God to punish him, and more, if he does not do what he says (3:17; 20:13; 25:22; Ruth 1:17). The Hebrew does not say "to me" here, though the oath implies it; the Greek translation adds it.

decisions.choice: for surely you will die: Saul binds himself to kill his son
decisions.reason: This is Saul's third oath of the day (verses 24, 39). Each has made his position harder.

decisions.choice: deal with me; punish me
decisions.reason: Balanced and Readable state the self-curse plainly, supplying "me", which the oath form implies.

source.text: וַיֹּ֨אמֶר הָעָ֜ם אֶל־שָׁא֗וּל הֲֽיוֹנָתָ֤ן׀יָמוּת֙ אֲשֶׁ֣ר עָ֠שָׂה הַיְשׁוּעָ֨ה הַגְּדוֹלָ֣ה הַזֹּאת֮ בְּיִשְׂרָאֵל֒ חָלִ֗ילָה חַי־יְהוָה֙ אִם־יִפֹּ֞ל מִשַּׂעֲרַ֤ת רֹאשׁוֹ֙ אַ֔רְצָה כִּֽי־עִם־אֱלֹהִ֥ים עָשָׂ֖ה הַיּ֣וֹם הַזֶּ֑ה וַיִּפְדּ֥וּ הָעָ֛ם אֶת־יוֹנָתָ֖ן וְלֹא־מֵֽת׃ס

records.literal_gloss: And said the people to Saul, Will Jonathan die, who has done this great deliverance in Israel? Far be it! [As] Yahweh lives, not will fall from [the] hair of his head to the ground, for with God he has worked this day. And ransomed the people Jonathan, and not he died.

en.L: And the people said to Saul, "Shall Jonathan die, who has worked this great deliverance in Israel? Far from it! [As] {{divine_name:the LORD|Yahweh}} lives, not one hair of his head will fall to the ground, for he has worked with God this day." So the people ransomed Jonathan, and he did not die.
en.B: But the troops said to Saul, "Should Jonathan die, when he has brought about this great deliverance in Israel? Never! As surely as {{divine_name:the LORD|Yahweh}} lives, not one hair of his head will fall to the ground, for he has done this today with God's help." So the troops ransomed Jonathan, and he did not die.
en.R: But the men said to Saul, "Jonathan is the one who won this great victory for Israel! Should he die? No! As surely as {{divine_name:the LORD|Yahweh}} lives, not even one hair of his head will fall to the ground. God helped him do what he did today!" So the men saved Jonathan's life, and he did not die.

decisions.choice: deliverance: rescue from the enemy, victory in battle
decisions.reason: The word is used of Yahweh's rescue of his people in war (11:13; Exodus 14:13). The troops give Jonathan the credit for being the one through whom it came.

decisions.choice: not a hair of his head will fall to the ground: he will not be harmed at all
decisions.reason: The same oath protects a person completely elsewhere (2 Samuel 14:11; 1 Kings 1:52). The troops answer Saul's oath with an oath of their own.

decisions.choice: with God he has worked: God acted with Jonathan
decisions.reason: The troops see that God was on Jonathan's side that day, as Jonathan himself had hoped (verse 6). A man God has worked with cannot be under God's curse.

decisions.choice: ransomed: set free by paying a price or giving a substitute
decisions.reason: The verb is used of buying back a firstborn or an animal by payment or substitute (Exodus 13:13; Numbers 18:15). The text does not say how the troops ransomed Jonathan, whether by an offering, a payment, or simply by their own stand against Saul.

decisions.choice: won this great victory; saved Jonathan's life
decisions.reason: Readable uses everyday words for "deliverance" and "ransomed"; see m1 and m4.

source.text: וַיַּ֣עַל שָׁא֔וּל מֵאַחֲרֵ֖י פְּלִשְׁתִּ֑ים וּפְלִשְׁתִּ֖ים הָלְכ֥וּ לִמְקוֹמָֽם׃

records.literal_gloss: And went up Saul from after [the] Philistines, and [the] Philistines went to their place.

en.L: And Saul went up from [pursuing] after the Philistines, and the Philistines went to their own place.
en.B: Then Saul stopped pursuing the Philistines and went back up, and the Philistines returned to their own land.
en.R: Then Saul stopped chasing the Philistines and went home. And the Philistines went back to their own land.

decisions.choice: went up from after the Philistines: gave up the pursuit
decisions.reason: Saul climbs back into the hill country and leaves off chasing the enemy. The night attack he planned (verse 36) never happens.

decisions.choice: the Philistines went to their place: the victory is left unfinished
decisions.reason: Jonathan had said that the oath kept the victory from being greater (verse 30). The Philistines go home to fight again (verse 52).

decisions.choice: their own land
decisions.reason: Balanced and Readable say "land" for "place", meaning the Philistine territory on the coast.

source.text: וְשָׁא֛וּל לָכַ֥ד הַמְּלוּכָ֖ה עַל־יִשְׂרָאֵ֑ל וַיִּלָּ֣חֶם סָבִ֣יב׀בְּֽכָל־אֹיְבָ֡יו בְּמוֹאָ֣ב׀וּבִבְנֵי־עַמּ֨וֹן וּבֶאֱד֜וֹם וּבְמַלְכֵ֤י צוֹבָה֙ וּבַפְּלִשְׁתִּ֔ים וּבְכֹ֥ל אֲשֶׁר־יִפְנֶ֖ה יַרְשִֽׁיעַ׃
